 View Comments Sutton officials said they are still considering a proposal from the Kraft Group to build a massive data center in the town. MARK STOCKWELL FOR THE BOSTON GLOBE After igniting a firestorm of criticism from residents over a massive data center proposed by two Kraft family companies, officials in the Central Massachusetts town of Sutton declared Friday that they are not backing away from the prospect. 
 In a lengthy, unsigned statement posted on Sutton’s web site, the town said it recognized “significant public interest in, and concerns about, the potential development of a data center project.” 
 The statement also implies that potential financial gains for the town are what’s keeping officials at the table: “Responsible municipal leadership means evaluating opportunities that could strengthen Sutton’s financial future while protecting the character, resources, and quality of life residents value.” 
 The controversy erupted Monday, when the town manager sent a memo to Sutton’s five-member Select Board outlining a proposal from the Kraft Group and its Unified Global Packaging Group business to build a massive data center – one that would be among the largest in the country – on a parcel of industrial property on the north side of town. More than 100 residents jammed a board meeting Tuesday night to express concerns about excessive electricity and water usage, noise pollution, and other potential problems that such a large facility could bring to this rural community.

Enter Email Sign Up Seething Sutton residents attack Kraft data center plans in first public forum The proposed project would include 10 buildings, erected on land owned by the Krafts’ Unified Packaging box business about 10 miles south of Worcester. Under the rough proposal disclosed Monday, the Kraft Group would build a $16 billion data center campus that would require up to 900 megawatts of electricity, enough to power a sizable city. The project would include 10 buildings, erected on land owned by Unified Packaging, about 10 miles south of Worcester. 
 After several days of continuing anger and organizing against the data center project by residents, town officials broke their silence on Friday with the posted statement, which outlined the required process for such a project to move forward. 
 “Considering an opportunity is not the same as supporting it,” the statement noted. “Our obligation is to understand it fully: its potential benefits, its potential costs, and its potential impacts on the residents and resources that make Sutton the community it is. Only with that understanding can the Town, and ultimately Town Meeting, make an informed decision.” 
 The Kraft Group issued a statement Thursday night to the Globe, billing the potential data center as “an opportunity to bring meaningful long-term economic investment to Sutton.” Addressing the criticisms from residents, the Kraft Group pledged “to working collaboratively with local officials, residents and other stakeholders,” adding: “this project will only move forward if the community and the Town of Sutton want it.” 
 Sutton does not have a zoning bylaw that pertains to data centers, meaning the town, through its Select Board, Zoning Board, and Town Meeting, would have to draft and approve zoning language before any project could move forward. The process could take “several months of review and public discussion,” per the statement. A zoning amendment would have to be approved by a two-thirds majority of Sutton’s Town Meeting. 
 That meeting would likely take place in May, 2027, according to Town Manager Austin Cyganiewicz. In the meantime, town officials, Unified, and the Kraft Group will try to address residents’ concerns over water and power usage, as well as any environmental or health risks. 
 Cyganiewicz did not respond to a request for comment Friday. 
 On Tuesday, he told the Globe he shared residents’ concerns brought up at the fiery Select Board meeting this week. As a resident of neighboring Millbury, Cyganiewicz said the project “will impact my community as well. So I want to make sure that whatever happens over the next several months … that it’s the best project for the Town of Sutton and the region.” 
 Despite the concerns that have been raised, a $16 billion data center could help alleviate the town’s precarious financial situation. The data center could bring in $10 million in taxes in 2031 and close to $30 million by 2035, according to Cyganiewicz’s Monday memo. 
 Otherwise, Sutton is hurtling toward a budget deficit of about $350,000 in its fiscal year starting in July, projected to grow to $2.5 million in the following budget cycle, and reaching about $10 million by 2033, the memo noted. Massachusetts municipalities are required by law to balance their budgets every year, so Sutton could be faced with cutting services and laying off teachers or other town workers in the years ahead. 
 “Revenue is simply not matching what we’re anticipating for expenses,” the town manager said at an October presentation to the Select Board. “Unfortunately, this would mean a reduction in services across most, if not all, of our departments.” 
 Sutton officials attributed the ballooning deficits to Proposition 2 1⁄2, a state law that generally prohibits towns from raising their property tax revenue by more than 2.5 percent per year, excluding new growth, unless voters approve a larger increase. With the costs for everything from diesel fuel to health insurance rising at much faster rates, that’s put towns like Sutton in hot pursuit of new commercial projects that can bring in more tax revenue beyond the cap. 
 “If there was a major commercial enterprise or a cluster of commercial enterprises that could help spike our revenue and not drive our cost,” Select Board Member Jim Ettamarna said at the October meeting, five weeks before the data center proposal landed on the board’s desk. 
 Unified Packaging has been working with the town over the past five years to develop the 383-acre parcel, formerly the site of a cement factory and a gravel pit, where the data center campus would be located. It has already opened a large commercial building and is constructing another on the property, though both would be dwarfed by the data center project. The company had earlier hoped to build a large warehouse on the parcel, but when those plans fell through, a member of the Sutton Select Board last year suggested a smaller type of data center as a possibility. 
 Residents of Sutton and abutting towns have swiftly organized in staunch opposition to the project. This week, Sutton resident Candice Edwards launched a Facebook group that reached nearly 400 members by Friday. And community members in Millbury also have spoken against the project before their town officials. Edwards’ coalition is pooling resources and volunteers with legal, scientific, or local government expertise. She described it as a “David vs. Goliath” type battle. 
 “The decisions being made today are going to impact our children’s future tomorrow,” said Edwards, mother of an 11-year-old. 
 Separately, a signature-collecting campaign started Thursday for a new ballot measure in 2028. The proposed question would introduce restrictions statewide on new data center projects, such as municipal protections for electricity price shifts, water permits, and town approval. The proposal was filed by the Committee to Restrict Data Centers, chaired by Jim Fleming , a political organizer with past experience in signature-gathering campaigns. 
 Friday’s Sutton statement said no town officials had signed nondisclosure agreements related to the proposal, and that Sutton had created a web page that will include public information and materials about the project.
